Inference

/IN-fur-uhns/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Inference means a judgment worked out from evidence and reasoning rather than something directly observed or stated

Inference means a judgment worked out from evidence and reasoning rather than something directly observed or stated

Worked Example

Watching the harbor flags snap straight out and the gulls streaming inland, the old sailor made a quick <strong style="color:var(--accent);">inference</strong>: a storm would reach the coast before nightfall.

No forecast told the sailor about the storm; he reasoned it out from clues — the stiff wind and the fleeing birds. A judgment built from evidence like that is an inference.

How Inference Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

deduction

deduction: an answer that follows strictly from the evidence by logic

extrapolation

extrapolation: an estimate that extends known facts into the unknown

interpretation

interpretation: an explanation of what something means

Antonyms

observation

observation: a fact taken in directly with the senses, not reasoned out

fact

fact: something known directly and certainly, needing no reasoning

How Strong Is It? — hunch → inference → proof

hunch vs. inference

hunch vs. inference: A hunch is a gut feeling with nothing behind it; an inference stands on actual evidence.

proof vs. inference

proof vs. inference: Proof is stronger than an inference — it settles the matter, while an inference can still turn out wrong.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of inference.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: in, into

Root — -fer-

Root — -fer-: to carry, bring (Latin ferre)

Suffix — -ence

Suffix — -ence: state or result of

Put it together

Put it together: An in-fer-ence is what gets 'carried in' from the evidence — the result you bring back after reasoning your way through the clues.

Use the root in a new word: fertile

Use the root in a new word: fertile: The fertile river valley produced three harvests a year — soil that literally 'carries' crop after crop.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral / academic

The classic collocation is to draw an inference. Science classes contrast an inference (reasoned from evidence) with an observation (seen directly) — keep the two apart. This is the noun partner of the verb infer, taught in this same unit: you infer, and the result is an inference.
